newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African parties seek allies to take on giant ANC.
newsitem.headline: S.African parties seek allies to take on giant ANC.

text.p: South Africa's opposition parties, eyes already on the 1999 national elections, are scrambling around for new alliances to take on the might of President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress.
The white-led National Party, the Zulu-based Inkatha Freedom Party and smaller groups said on Monday they were bargaining and manoeuvring to find their best way to fight Mandela's monolith.

"The ANC is becoming stronger all the time. If it develops into one-party dominance, that is not in the interests of democracy," said Fanus Schoeman, a spokesman for former president F.W. de Klerk's Nationalists.
The party that invented apartheid said it would talk to other groups sharing its conservative values to try to forge a new movement, probably with a new name to break with the past.
Parties say the political landscape that got South Africa through its critical first all-race elections in 1994 cannot survive for long and is in need of a radical overhaul.
The ANC is too big, trying to please diverse groups, and the others are too small, unable to mount a real challenge and struggling to widen their narrow race-based support.
The NP's bid last year to forge closer ties with Inkatha, which espouses similar free-market and federalist policies, made little apparent headway.
When the NP quit Mandela's national unity government in June, saying it was being ignored, Inkatha stayed on.
It has kept a sharply distinct identity, thanks to its leader, Zulu chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi, but failed to spread its support far beyond the Zulus of KwaZulu-Natal province.
Buthelezi's two top officials, chairman Frank Mdlalose and secretary-general Ziba Jiyane, said at the weekend they were resigning, plunging Inkatha into its worst crisis since 1994.
Party sources blamed friction with hardline Buthelezi, who nearly boycotted the 1994 poll and who they say has blocked overtures to the ANC to end bloody inter-party conflict.

Inkatha may be joined in South Africa's ANC-led ruling coalition by two smaller parties, the white-led liberal Democrats (DP) and leftist Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), who hope similarly to raise their profiles without compromising their role as opposition forces.
The PAC said this month it had agreed in principle to join the cabinet after an offer from Mandela, who called for a patriotic front of democratic forces in South Africa.
Some say a PAC-DP-Inkatha front within government that is under discussion could turn the NP into a political wallflower.
"It would break the racial mould of South African politics and leave the NP out on a limb," wrote the Sunday Independent.
But the NP brushed aside gloomy predictions of its fate.

Although it has so far failed to bury its tainted past and appeal to the black majority, Schoeman said the party was committed to breaking the racial mould of South African politics, and this was the aim of its search for partners.
"It is a difficult thing to do, but it is very necessary that we at least try and see if it is possible," he said.
Everyone knows the ANC, which polled around two-thirds of the vote last time, will win again in 1999 and take South Africa into its post-Mandela era led by his deputy, Thabo Mbeki.
Fissures within the ANC's mass ranks are swiftly dealt with as Mandela's former favourite Bantu Holomisa, a deputy minister, found last year when he was sacked for public dissent.
Holomisa has hinted he may start his own party but will face the full wrath of the ANC if he does, analysts say.
